item.title: From float parade to crown: Miss Hibiscus 2026 crowning set for tonight
item.description: The streets of Suva came alive this morning as the 70th FMF Hibiscus Festival reached its final day with a colourful float parade from the Suva Flea Market to Albert Park. The parade brought together families, supporters, contestants and members of the public as generations of Fijians came out to celebrate one of the country’s longest-running and most cherished festivals.
item.content:encoded:
The streets of Suva came alive this morning as the 70th FMF Hibiscus Festival reached its final day with a colourful float parade from the Suva Flea Market to Albert Park.

The parade brought together families, supporters, contestants and members of the public as generations of Fijians came out to celebrate one of the country’s longest-running and most cherished festivals.

For seven decades, the Hibiscus Festival has been part of Fiji’s cultural and social fabric, creating memories for generations of people who have grown up attending its events, cheering on contestants and enjoying the celebrations.

This morning’s float parade added another vibrant chapter to that history, with colourful floats making their way through the streets of Suva as the city marked the final day of this year’s celebrations.

The excitement will continue this hour, when the winners of Best Float, Miss Personality, Miss Photogenic and Miss People’s Choice will be announced, alongside the crowning of Miss Charity.

The biggest moment of the festival will come tonight, with the announcement of the first and second runners-up, followed by the crowning of Miss Hibiscus 2026 from 6.30pm to 8pm.

item.title: Second chance at life for PSH head chef
item.description: It was a moment of relief for 33-year-old Rishil Ravnit Kumar, head chef at Pacific Specialist Healthcare Hospital, after PSH founder and Chief Executive Officer Parvish Kumar offered to personally cover the cost of his heart treatment. item.content:encoded:
It was a moment of relief for 33-year-old Rishil Ravnit Kumar, head chef at Pacific Specialist Healthcare Hospital, after PSH founder and Chief Executive Officer Parvish Kumar offered to personally cover the cost of his heart treatment.

Kumar says he discovered that he needed heart bypass surgery when he underwent an echocardiogram and angiogram after experiencing severe chest pains and shortness of breath.

However, Kumar says he was unable to afford the surgery at short notice but is grateful for the support, which he describes as giving him a second chance at life.

Kumar says he initially consulted PSH interventional cardiologist Dr Srikar Miryala, who conducted the necessary tests along with the hospital's heart team, including consultant cardiologist Dr Omar Niazi and cardiothoracic and vascular surgeon Dr Sanjeev Kumar Khulbey, who recommended Total Arterial Revascularisation and Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting, commonly known as heart bypass surgery, rather than angioplasty or stenting.

The head chef says he underwent surgery on May 12 and was back on his feet and walking normally three days later.

Kumar says he is now fully recovered and has returned to work as the hospital's head chef.

He has also thanked the hospital's cardiologists and ICU team for caring for him before and after the surgery.

Meanwhile, PSH Hospitals founder and CEO Parvish Kumar says the successful surgery demonstrates the capability of the hospital's heart team to perform complex cardiac procedures.

item.title: Young Fijians learn traditional skills to keep iTaukei culture alive

item.content:encoded:
The Fiji Museum, in collaboration with the Veiqia Project, is conducting a Masi Printing and Liku Weaving Workshop, where local artists like Laijipa Sukulu from Moce , Lau, and Joana Veitala from Tawav a, Yawe , Kadavu are guiding children through the traditional practices and teaching them how they are done.

One of the participants, Fareesha Ahemad, says she attended the workshop with two of her siblings because she wanted to learn more about iTaukei culture.

Fareesha says taking part in activities such as masi printing was a new experience for her and gave her an opportunity to learn something she had not done before.

She says learning about different cultures can also help young people make new friends, better understand each other and become more involved in the wider Fijian community.

Fareesha says she hopes to take what she has learnt from the workshop back to her friends at school and at home and encourage them to learn how traditional items are made.

She says it is important for young people to take an interest in these skills as traditional cultural knowledge and practices risk fading if they are not passed on to younger generations.

Another participant, Vivek Tushal Prasad from Suva, says this was his first time learning about masi and his mother encouraged him to take part in the workshop.

Prasad says it is important for the younger generation to learn traditional skills now as the knowledge could be useful to them as they grow older.

He says being part of the Indo-Fijian community while learning about iTaukei customs has also given him an opportunity to understand how iTaukei people traditionally lived and carried out cultural practices.

Prasad says learning about another community's culture can also teach young people the importance of respecting other cultures and being kind to one another.

He is encouraging other young people to take an interest in the cultures and traditions around them rather than allowing the knowledge of their forefathers to disappear.

Fareesha also believes workshops like this can help keep ancestral knowledge alive by giving children the opportunity to learn traditional skills and eventually pass them on to others.

item.title: Educators look to make literature lessons more meaningful and engaging for children
item.description: Educators, teachers and teacher trainees are exploring new and meaningful ways of teaching literature to children and young people through an inaugural Literature Teaching Workshop held at Fiji National University’s (FNU) Natabua Campus in Lautoka. The two-day workshop, which began on Thursday, was hosted by the Office of the Dean of the College of Humanities, Education and Law (CHEL), through the
item.content:encoded:
Educators, teachers and teacher trainees are exploring new and meaningful ways of teaching literature to children and young people through an inaugural Literature Teaching Workshop held at Fiji National University’s (FNU) Natabua Campus in Lautoka.

The two-day workshop, which began on Thursday, was hosted by the Office of the Dean of the College of Humanities, Education and Law (CHEL), through the School of Communication, Language and Literature (SCLL).

Held under the theme, “Transforming the Teaching of Literature (ECE–Primary–Secondary),” the workshop brought together academics, pre-service teachers and students from across CHEL.

The programme focused on innovative approaches to literature teaching across early childhood, primary and secondary education, while encouraging educators to consider how literature can help children better understand themselves and the world around them.

Chief Guest Professor Margaret Sims of Macquarie University, who is also an Adjunct Professor with FNU’s CHEL, highlighted the importance of carefully selecting literature that helps children develop knowledge, values and perspectives.

She says meaningful literature does not always have to come from glossy, published books, but could also come from children’s own experiences, families and communities.

She also stressed the importance of considering the emotional impact of literature on children and exposing them to stories that reflect a range of lives and experiences.

Professor Sims says literature can help children consider what it might feel like to live in another person’s circumstances, allowing them to develop a deeper understanding of different experiences.

Head of the School of Communication, Language and Literature Suzie Aziz says the workshop encouraged educators to reflect on how literature could be taught in ways that go beyond simply reading texts.

She says educators should consider how they could encourage students to experience, question and connect with literature while discovering meaning through texts.

Aziz says educators must continue adapting their teaching approaches to meet the needs of today's learners, while preserving the richness and value of literature.

She adds that literature play an important role in shaping how children experience reading, storytelling and learning throughout their lives.

item.title: Uni student penalised after being caught wearing smart glasses in test
item.description: A University of Auckland student has been penalised after being caught wearing smart glasses during a test, raising fresh concerns over how emerging technology could be used by students to cheat. The incident has highlighted the challenges universities may face as smart glasses become increasingly accessible, with some models equipped with cameras and artificial intelligence features.
item.content:encoded:
A University of Auckland student has been penalised after being caught wearing smart glasses during a test, raising fresh concerns over how emerging technology could be used by students to cheat.

The incident has highlighted the challenges universities may face as smart glasses become increasingly accessible, with some models equipped with cameras and artificial intelligence features.

University of Auckland Computer Science Senior Lecturer Ulrich Speidel says smart glasses can potentially allow students to record exam questions, send them to outside helpers or AI systems, and receive information directly through the glasses.

A University of Auckland spokesperson says the student was seen wearing smart glasses during a test by an invigilator, despite a pre-test announcement explicitly stating that smart glasses and watches were not permitted.

The glasses were removed and the student was allowed to continue the test.

The university says an academic integrity investigation was carried out and the student received a penalty, although it would not disclose what the penalty was.

Speidel says exam invigilators will now need to be increasingly alert to students using smart glasses.

He says some smart glasses can be identified by their broad hinge sections or larger bridges.

Invigilators could also ask students to cover the cameras with masking tape, particularly when the glasses are prescription eyewear.

The concerns come as smart glasses become more widely available.

The University of Auckland says it will continue to monitor emerging technologies as part of its efforts to uphold academic integrity.

item.title: No one charged yet in alleged overseas employment scam involving more than 300 Fijians
item.description: Crystal Robanakadavu · 04/09/2026 Police had earlier confirmed to fijivillage News that a report has been lodged at the Namaka Police Station and an investigation is underway.
item.content:encoded:
Crystal Robanakadavu · 04/09/2026

Police had earlier confirmed to fijivillage News that a report has been lodged at the Namaka Police Station and an investigation is underway.

More than 300 people claim they paid $100 each after being promised overseas employment opportunities, with some expecting to travel to Australia.

They say over 50 people reportedly turned up at the Nadi International Airport last Saturday expecting to travel overseas but later discovered that there were no flight bookings for them.

Some of those affected had reportedly resigned from their jobs in preparation for the promised overseas employment.

The Ministry of Employment is urging those affected to lodge reports with Police and stresses that workers are not required to pay recruitment fees to participate in Government-facilitated overseas employment programmes.

item.title: Doctors urge Fijians not to wait for heart attack symptoms to worsen
item.description: Fijians are being urged not to wait until chest pain becomes unbearable before seeking medical attention, with cardiologists warning that delayed treatment can lead to more serious heart damage and complications. As Fiji observes World Heart Month under the 2026 theme, "Don't Miss a Beat", Interventional cardiologist Dr Srikar Miryala says many patients seek specialist care only after their condit
item.content:encoded:
Fijians are being urged not to wait until chest pain becomes unbearable before seeking medical attention, with cardiologists warning that delayed treatment can lead to more serious heart damage and complications.

As Fiji observes World Heart Month under the 2026 theme, "Don't Miss a Beat", Interventional cardiologist Dr Srikar Miryala says many patients seek specialist care only after their condition has significantly deteriorated or they have already suffered a heart attack.

He says recognising symptoms early and seeking immediate medical attention can improve treatment options and outcomes.

Dr Miryala says early intervention can sometimes allow patients to undergo less invasive procedures such as angioplasty or stenting.

Since March last year, he has been performing primary, or emergency, percutaneous coronary intervention procedures at PSH Hospitals.

The procedure is used to restore blood flow during a serious heart attack caused by the complete blockage of a major coronary artery, helping to minimise damage to the heart.

Dr Miryala also says substance abuse and high consumption of kava and fizzy drinks are among the other concerns contributing to heart disease in Fiji.

Award-winning cardiothoracic and vascular surgeon Dr Sanjeev Kumar Khulbey echoed the same sentiments saying that lifestyle choices are also contributing to Fijians developing heart-related conditions at younger ages.

With 30 years of experience as a cardiac specialist, Dr Khulbey says people, particularly those over 40, need to take greater responsibility for monitoring their health.

He says Fiji has access to fresh fish, fruits and vegetables, yet many people continue to rely on canned and processed foods.

According to Dr Khulbey, heart disease can be linked to lifestyle choices, existing medical conditions and genetics, although many risk factors can be reduced through healthier eating, regular exercise, avoiding tobacco and limiting alcohol consumption.

He says every household should also have a blood pressure monitor and blood sugar monitor to help people regularly keep track of their health.

Dr Khulbey is also warning people against relying on herbal medicines or homemade remedies when they are unwell, urging them to seek professional medical advice instead.
